# Summary

We compare a dummy classifier, a decision tree, logistic regression, and a support vector classifier on a seven-class weight-status prediction task. The models use demographic, family history, and lifestyle variables from the UCI Obesity Levels dataset, with height and weight excluded. About 77% of the published records are synthetic, which limits what performance on this dataset can tell us about performance on independently collected survey data.

<!-- Add the selected model, its held-out test score, a comparison with the dummy baseline, and the main implication. Keep the final summary to one paragraph. -->

# Introduction

Researchers have compared machine learning models for classifying weight status from survey data, including models that use both eating habits and physical measurements  (Kaur et al. 2022 and Solomon et al. 2023). For this dataset, the authors calculated body mass index (BMI) from height and weight and used it to assign the weight-status labels (Mendoza Palechor and de la Hoz Manotas, 2019). Excluding those measurements and any features derived from them lets us test how much predictive information comes from the remaining survey responses.

Our research question is: **How well can demographic, family history, and lifestyle features predict the seven weight-status categories when height and weight are excluded, and which of the four classifiers performs best?** Comparing the classifiers against a dummy baseline shows whether using these survey responses improves predictions over a simple benchmark.

We use the UCI Obesity Levels dataset (UCI Machine Learning Repository 2019), which contains 2,111 records based on an online survey conducted in Mexico, Peru, and Colombia. Each row describes one individual or is a synthetic record generated from the survey data. The candidate predictors include age, gender, family history of overweight, eating habits, physical activity, and other behaviours such as usual transportation. The response is the recorded weight-status category, which includes insufficient weight, normal weight, overweight levels I and II, and obesity types I, II, and III.

# Methods

## Data
We used the Estimation of Obesity Levels Based on Eating Habits and Physical Condition data set from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (UCI Machine Learning Repository 2019; Mendoza Palechor and de la Hoz Manotas 2019). The code below downloads the original archive into data/raw/ and reads the data file. Each row contains one individual’s survey responses about demographics, family history, eating habits and physical condition, together with a weight-status category. About 77% of the rows are synthetic records that the data set’s authors generated to balance the classes.

Because the original authors assigned the weight-status categories by calculating body mass index (BMI) from height and weight, we removed both of these variables before any analysis. Keeping them would allow a model to recover the label almost directly, rather than learning from lifestyle and demographic information. We then split the data into a training set (70%) and a test set (30%), stratified by weight-status category so that both sets have the same class proportions, with a fixed random seed for reproducibility. The two sets are saved to data/processed/. All exploratory analysis, preprocessing decisions and model selection used the training set only. The test set was used once, for the final evaluation

```{python}
# Create the data folders if they don't exist
os.makedirs("../data/raw", exist_ok=True)
os.makedirs("../data/processed", exist_ok=True)

csv_path = "../data/raw/ObesityDataSet_raw_and_data_sinthetic.csv"

# Download data as zip and extract
# This archive (UCI "Estimation of Obesity Levels Based On Eating Habits and Physical Condition") also contains ObesityDataSet_raw_and_data_sinthetic.csv
if not os.path.exists(csv_path):
    url ="https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/544/estimation+of+obesity+levels+based+on+eating+habits+and+physical+condition.zip"

    request = requests.get(url)
    with open("../data/raw/estimation+of+obesity+levels+based+on+eating+habits+and+physical+condition.zip", 'wb') as f:
        f.write(request.content)

    with zipfile.ZipFile("../data/raw/estimation+of+obesity+levels+based+on+eating+habits+and+physical+condition.zip", 'r') as zip_ref:
        zip_ref.extractall("../data/raw")

    os.remove("../data/raw/estimation+of+obesity+levels+based+on+eating+habits+and+physical+condition.zip")

# Read in data
obesity = pd.read_csv(csv_path).drop(columns=["Height","Weight"])
```

```{python}
# Do the train/test split and save the results to data/processed/
set_config(transform_output="pandas")

# split the data into training (70%) and test (30%) sets
obesity_train, obesity_test = train_test_split(
    obesity, train_size=0.70, stratify=obesity["NObeyesdad"], random_state=522
)

obesity_train.to_csv("../data/processed/obesity_train.csv", index=False)
obesity_test.to_csv("../data/processed/obesity_test.csv", index=False)
```

## Analysis

Age and the five survey-scale features (vegetable consumption frequency, number of main meals per day, daily water intake, physical activity frequency and time using technology devices) were treated as numeric variables and standardized. Although these survey questions were answered on short integer scales, most values in the data set are not whole numbers because of the synthetic records, so treating them as categories would not be appropriate. The remaining features (gender, family history of overweight, frequent consumption of high-calorie food, eating between meals, smoking, calorie monitoring, alcohol consumption and usual transportation) were one-hot encoded, ignoring any category not seen during training. All preprocessing steps were combined with each model in a scikit-learn pipeline, so that they were fit only on training data within each cross-validation fold.

The analysis was carried out using Python programming language (Van Rossum and Drake 2009), requests (Reitz 2011), zipfile (Van Rossum and Drake 2009), NumPy (Harris et al. 2020), pandas (McKinney 2010), Altair (VanderPlas et al. 2018) and scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al. 2011). Parts of the code used to perform the analysis and create this report were adapted from <https://github.com/UBC-MDS/DSCI_522_project-template-breast-cancer-predictor>.

```{python}
#Tentative preprocessing plan: standardize numeric features, one-hot encode binary and categorical features, and ordinal encode the two frequency features. The frequency features are ordered from least to most frequent.

# Reading the saved training and testing dataset files if dataframes not in memory
if "obesity_train" not in globals() or "obesity_test" not in globals():
    obesity_train = pd.read_csv("../data/processed/obesity_train.csv")
    obesity_test = pd.read_csv("../data/processed/obesity_test.csv")

# Group features by how they should be transformed
numeric_features = ["Age", "FCVC", "NCP", "CH2O", "FAF", "TUE"]
binary_features = ["Gender", "family_history_with_overweight", "FAVC", "SMOKE", "SCC"]
ordinal_features = ["CAEC", "CALC"]
categorical_features = ["MTRANS"]

# Order of the frequency categories (least to most)
frequency_levels = ["no", "Sometimes", "Frequently", "Always"]

# Make a column transformer that applies the appropriate transformation to each group of features. The remainder="passthrough" argument means that any features not listed in the groups will be passed through unchanged. 
obesity_preprocessor = make_column_transformer(
    (StandardScaler(), numeric_features),
    (OneHotEncoder(drop="if_binary", dtype=int, sparse_output=False), binary_features),
    (OrdinalEncoder(categories=[frequency_levels, frequency_levels]), ordinal_features),
    (OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False), categorical_features),
    remainder="passthrough"
)

# Fit on training data only, then transform both training and test data and save the results
obesity_preprocessor.fit(obesity_train)
scaled_obesity_train = obesity_preprocessor.transform(obesity_train)
scaled_obesity_test = obesity_preprocessor.transform(obesity_test)

scaled_obesity_train.to_csv("../data/processed/processed_obesity_train.csv", index=False)
scaled_obesity_test.to_csv("../data/processed/processed_obesity_test.csv", index=False)
```

## Model Selection

### Defining the models

We compare three classifiers:
- **Dummy Classifier**: Always predicting the most frequent class. Our baseline model.
- **Logistic Regressor**: Fast and interpretable linear model.
- **RBF Support Vector Classifier (SVC)**: Learns from non-linear decision boundaries.

Every model is placed in a pipeline with the preprocessor defined above to avoid leakage of validation folds into the encodings.

```{python}
#| label: define models

# Splitting the features and target
X_train = obesity_train.drop(columns="NObeyesdad")
y_train = obesity_train["NObeyesdad"]
X_test = obesity_test.drop(columns="NObeyesdad")
y_test = obesity_test["NObeyesdad"]

# Defining the models
models = {
    "Dummy": DummyClassifier(random_state=522),
    "Logistic Regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, random_state=522),
    "RBF SVC": SVC(random_state=522),
}

# clone() gives each pipeline its own unfitted copy of the preprocessor
pipelines = {
    name: make_pipeline(clone(obesity_preprocessor), model)
    for name, model in models.items()
}
```

### Evaluation Metric

- We select models using **macro-averaged F1**. F1 combines precision and recall for one class, and the macro average weights all seven weight-status classes equally, so a model that performs poorly on any one class is penalized. 
- We also report accuracy as a more familiar secondary measure. 
- @tbl-class-balance shows the training class proportions, which range from `{python} f"{y_train.value_counts(normalize=True).min():.1%}"` to `{python} f"{y_train.value_counts(normalize=True).max():.1%}"`. 
- The classes are close to balanced, so accuracy is not dominated by one class, but macro F1 still shows weakness on individual classes that accuracy can hide. 

Note: All model selection decisions below use macro F1 only.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-class-balance
#| tbl-cap: "Proportion of each weight-status class in the training set."

SCORING = {"f1_macro": "f1_macro", "accuracy": "accuracy"}  # selection uses f1_macro

# Same shuffled, stratified folds for every model
cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=522)

y_train.value_counts(normalize=True).round(3).rename("proportion").to_frame()
```

### Cross Validation and Hyperparameter Tuning

- All comparisons use five-fold stratified cross-validation on the training set only. 
- The dummy classifier has nothing to tune, so we cross-validate it directly. 
- For logistic regression and the SVC we use `RandomizedSearchCV` with 20 sampled candidates each, scored by validation macro F1. `C` and `gamma` can matter across several orders of magnitude, so we sample them from log-uniform distributions. Random search covers the continuous space at a fixed cost and avoids committing to a coarse grid. With `refit` enabled, each search refits its best candidate on the whole training set. The test set is not used at this stage.

```{python}
#| label: tune-models

# Baseline: cross-validated directly
dummy_cv = cross_validate(
    pipelines["Dummy"], X_train, y_train,
    cv=cv, scoring=SCORING, return_train_score=True,
)

# Search spaces (pipeline step name + "__" + parameter name)
param_dists = {
    "Logistic Regression": {"logisticregression__C": loguniform(1e-3, 1e2)},
    "RBF SVC": {
        "svc__C": loguniform(1e-2, 1e3),
        "svc__gamma": loguniform(1e-3, 1e1),
    },
}

searches = {}
for name, dist in param_dists.items():
    searches[name] = RandomizedSearchCV(
        pipelines[name], dist,
        n_iter=20, cv=cv, scoring=SCORING, refit="f1_macro",
        return_train_score=True, random_state=522,
    )
    searches[name].fit(X_train, y_train)
```

# Results

## Model Comparison

@tbl-cv-results shows the cross-validation results for the dummy baseline and the best configuration found for each tuned model. "Validation" scores come from held-out folds inside the training set. They are not the final test scores.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cv-results
#| tbl-cap: "Five-fold cross-validation results on the training set (mean and standard deviation across folds)."

rows = {
    "Dummy": {
        "Validation macro F1 (mean)": dummy_cv["test_f1_macro"].mean(),
        "Validation macro F1 (SD)": dummy_cv["test_f1_macro"].std(),
        "Training macro F1 (mean)": dummy_cv["train_f1_macro"].mean(),
        "Validation accuracy (mean)": dummy_cv["test_accuracy"].mean(),
        "Best hyperparameters": "none",
    }
}
for name, s in searches.items():
    i, r = s.best_index_, s.cv_results_
    rows[name] = {
        "Validation macro F1 (mean)": r["mean_test_f1_macro"][i],
        "Validation macro F1 (SD)": r["std_test_f1_macro"][i],
        "Training macro F1 (mean)": r["mean_train_f1_macro"][i],
        "Validation accuracy (mean)": r["mean_test_accuracy"][i],
        "Best hyperparameters": str(
            {k.split("__")[-1]: float(f"{v:.3g}") for k, v in s.best_params_.items()}
        ),
    }

comparison = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
comparison.round(4)
```

- The Dummy baseline reaches a validation macro F1 of only `{python} f"{dummy_cv['test_f1_macro'].mean():.3f}"`, so the survey responses carry predictive information beyond the class frequencies. <!-- Add one sentence comparing Logistic Regression and RBF SVC using @tbl-cv-results, and mention whether the gap is larger than the fold standard deviation. -->
- The RBF SVC clearly outperforms logistic regression, with a mean validation macro F1 of `{python} f"{comparison.loc['RBF SVC', 'Validation macro F1 (mean)']:.3f}"` versus `{python} f"{comparison.loc['Logistic Regression', 'Validation macro F1 (mean)']:.3f}"`. 
- The difference of `{python} f"{comparison.loc['RBF SVC', 'Validation macro F1 (mean)'] - comparison.loc['Logistic Regression', 'Validation macro F1 (mean)']:.3f}"` is more than ten times the fold standard deviation of either model (`{python} f"{comparison.loc['RBF SVC', 'Validation macro F1 (SD)']:.3f}"` for the SVC and `{python} f"{comparison.loc['Logistic Regression', 'Validation macro F1 (SD)']:.3f}"` for logistic regression), so the gap is not explained by fold-to-fold variation. 
- Validation accuracy shows the same ordering. Logistic regression's training score (`{python} f"{comparison.loc['Logistic Regression', 'Training macro F1 (mean)']:.3f}"`) is close to its validation score, which suggests that a linear model cannot capture the structure in these features. 
- The SVC fits the training data almost perfectly (training macro F1 of `{python} f"{comparison.loc['RBF SVC', 'Training macro F1 (mean)']:.3f}"`), so it overfits to some degree. Even so, it generalizes much better to the validation folds.

## Selected Model

We select the tuned model with the highest mean validation macro F1. The dummy is excluded because it is only a baseline.

```{python}
#| label: select-best-model

best_name = max(searches, key=lambda n: searches[n].best_score_)
best_search = searches[best_name]
i = best_search.best_index_

best_cv_f1 = best_search.best_score_
best_cv_sd = best_search.cv_results_["std_test_f1_macro"][i]
best_train_f1 = best_search.cv_results_["mean_train_f1_macro"][i]
best_params = {k.split("__")[-1]: float(f"{v:.3g}") for k, v in best_search.best_params_.items()}
dummy_f1 = dummy_cv["test_f1_macro"].mean()

print(best_name, best_params)
```

The selected model is **`{python} best_name`**, with a mean validation macro F1 of `{python} f"{best_cv_f1:.3f}"` (SD `{python} f"{best_cv_sd:.3f}"` across folds) against `{python} f"{dummy_f1:.3f}"` for the dummy baseline. Its training macro F1 is `{python} f"{best_train_f1:.3f}"`, so the gap between training and validation scores is `{python} f"{best_train_f1 - best_cv_f1:.3f}"`. The selected hyperparameters are `{python} str(best_params)`. 

## Fit and Test

Having chosen the model and its hyperparameters using training data only, we fit this pipeline once on the full training set and evaluate it once on the held-out test set. The test results were not used to change any modelling choice.

```{python}
#| label: final-fit-and-test

# Final fit: best pipeline + best hyperparameters, fitted on all training data
final_model = clone(pipelines[best_name]).set_params(**best_search.best_params_)
final_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# One-time evaluation on the held-out test set
y_pred = final_model.predict(X_test)
test_f1 = f1_score(y_test, y_pred, average="macro")
test_acc = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)

# Baseline on the same test set, for context only (not used for selection)
dummy_test_f1 = f1_score(
    y_test, clone(pipelines["Dummy"]).fit(X_train, y_train).predict(X_test), average="macro"
)

print(f"{best_name}: test macro F1 = {test_f1:.3f}, test accuracy = {test_acc:.3f}")
```

## Final Results

On the test set, the final **`{python} best_name`** model achieves a macro F1 of **`{python} f"{test_f1:.3f}"`** and an accuracy of `{python} f"{test_acc:.3f}"`, compared with a macro F1 of `{python} f"{dummy_test_f1:.3f}"` for the dummy baseline. This is close to the cross-validated estimate of `{python} f"{best_cv_f1:.3f}"`, a difference of `{python} f"{test_f1 - best_cv_f1:+.3f}"`. @tbl-test-report gives per-class performance, and @fig-confusion shows which classes are confused.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-test-report
#| tbl-cap: "Per-class precision, recall and F1 on the held-out test set."

order = ["Insufficient_Weight", "Normal_Weight", "Overweight_Level_I",
         "Overweight_Level_II", "Obesity_Type_I", "Obesity_Type_II", "Obesity_Type_III"]

report = pd.DataFrame(
    classification_report(y_test, y_pred, labels=order, output_dict=True, zero_division=0)
).T
report.loc[order + ["macro avg"], ["precision", "recall", "f1-score", "support"]].round(3)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-confusion
#| fig-cap: "Confusion matrix on the held-out test set. Rows are observed classes and columns are predicted classes, ordered from lowest to highest weight status."

cm = pd.crosstab(y_test, y_pred, rownames=["observed"], colnames=["predicted"]).reindex(
    index=order, columns=order, fill_value=0
)
cm_long = cm.reset_index().melt(id_vars="observed", var_name="predicted", value_name="count")

base = alt.Chart(cm_long).encode(
    x=alt.X("predicted:N", sort=order, title="Predicted class"),
    y=alt.Y("observed:N", sort=order, title="Observed class"),
)
heatmap = base.mark_rect().encode(color=alt.Color("count:Q", title="Count"))
labels = base.mark_text().encode(
    text="count:Q",
    color=alt.condition(alt.datum.count > cm.values.max() / 2, alt.value("white"), alt.value("black")),
)
(heatmap + labels).properties(width=200, height=200)
```

The most frequent errors involve `Normal_Weight`, which has the lowest F1 of any class (0.596, @tbl-test-report). Its recall is high (0.779), but its precision is only 0.482: the model predicted `Normal_Weight` for 139 test observations, and only 67 of them were truly normal weight. Many of the other classes' errors fall into this category (@fig-confusion), including 24 `Overweight_Level_I`, 16 `Overweight_Level_II`, 16 `Insufficient_Weight` and 13 `Obesity_Type_I` observations. The two overweight classes are the next weakest (F1 of 0.685 and 0.692). Most errors are between neighbouring categories, such as `Insufficient_Weight` and `Overweight_Level_I` predicted as `Normal_Weight`, and `Overweight_Level_II` confused with `Obesity_Type_I`. However, some observations skip categories, such as `Overweight_Level_II` and `Obesity_Type_I` predicted as `Normal_Weight`. In contrast, `Obesity_Type_II` and `Obesity_Type_III` are almost never confused with other classes (F1 of 0.943 and 0.990). This is plausible because the labels were defined from body mass index, which our models cannot see (height and weight were excluded), so people near a category boundary can have very similar survey responses.

Because about 77% of the records in this dataset are synthetic, these scores may be optimistic compared with performance on independently collected survey data.
